newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition, opposition spar in pensions debate.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition, opposition spar in pensions debate.

text.p: German Labour Minister Norbert Bluem's pensions reform bill came under heavy attack from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) at its first reading in the Bundestag lower house of parliament on Friday.
The bill plans phased cuts in a typical state pension to 64 percent of average net pay from 1999 on from 70 percent now.

Bluem said he would share out fairly the extra costs of the pay-as-you-go system arising from the "greying" of the German population. The average German draws a pension for nearly 16 years, compared to 10 years in 1960, he said.
But opposition deputies said that planned cuts in pensions amounted to a breach of solidarity between young and old.
"Do you think that the pensioners of today and the future do not notice that?" SPD social affairs spokesman Rudolf Dressler said, in remarks directed at Bluem.
Bluem's bill falls short of advocating drastic reform, and instead tinkers by removing some non-welfare items from the state pensions fund.
Those would be covered by 15 billion marks ($8.7 billion) in annual federal budget transfers, leaving possible room for a cut in contributions from today's record 20.3 percent of wages.
The opposition Greens said they accepted the need to let pensions fall in relation to earnings, but called for higher federal cash transfers to be financed by higher petrol taxes.
Bluem said he had not given up hope of reaching a pensions consensus with the SPD, but added that the government would not shy away from legislating alone.
Unlike tax reforms also working their way through parliament, the SPD cannot block the pensions reform in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament.
